name: opentimestamps-client
why: Anchors proofs in Bitcoin's blockchain via Merkle trees; a real door into timestamping and a protocol few have examined.

brief.what_it_is: A command-line tool, written in Python, that creates and verifies OpenTimestamps proofs. You give it a file; it hashes the file and sends only the digest to remote calendar servers, which batch digests into Bitcoin transactions. The output is a .ots proof file that can be checked later against the Bitcoin blockchain. The same package can also timestamp PGP-signed Git commits and verify timestamps on whole commits or individual files in a Git repository. The installed commands are ots and ots-git-gpg-wrapper.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a way to use the Bitcoin blockchain as a timestamp notary, so anyone can prove that data existed at a given time without a trusted third party. The homepage says the project 'aims to be a standard format for blockchain timestamping.'
brief.how_it_works: Stamping hashes the file and submits the digest to one or more remote calendars, which return a pending proof, and the digest is committed to Bitcoin in a batched transaction. The README says the calendar only ever receives an opaque digest, with a per-file nonce protecting the contents. Verification needs the Bitcoin block header: until a calendar upgrades the proof with the path to that header, the proof reads as pending, and a local Bitcoin node can check it directly. The README does not use the phrase Merkle tree; the ots info output shows a chain of append, prepend and sha256 operations that the proof replays to reach the block.

commands_seen.context: Installs the client from PyPI (appears on both the homepage and the README).
Creates README.md.ots by submitting the file's digest to three remote calendars; the README shows the calendar URLs printed during submission.
Right after stamping, reports each calendar as 'Pending confirmation in Bitcoin blockchain'; confirmation takes a few hours.
Verifies a bundled example locally with no waiting; the README says it succeeds against Bitcoin block 358391, dated 2015-05-28.
Same check routed through a local Bitcoin Core node using JSON-RPC credentials in place of USER and PASS.
Shows an incomplete proof being completed by asking a remote calendar for the block-header path, then succeeding.
Adds the Bitcoin path to the proof itself so it no longer needs the calendar.
Prints the file's sha256 and the proof's commitment operations and attestations, for inspecting what a proof contains.
Installs from a source checkout instead of PyPI.
Homepage's Python quick-start line for stamping a file.

brief.install_notes: Needs Python 3. Install with pip3 install opentimestamps-client, or from source with python3 setup.py install. On Debian Stretch the README lists system packages: python3 python3-dev python3-pip python3-setuptools python3-wheel. Creating timestamps needs no Bitcoin node and no account or API key, since the default calendars are free. Verifying needs a local Bitcoin Core node (a pruned node is fine), or the calendars can complete proofs for you. The --bitcoin-node flag takes an RPC URL with credentials. The README warns that a conflicting 'bitcoin' pip package can break ots, and gives a fix: uninstall both bitcoin and python-bitcoinlib, delete the leftover bitcoin directory from dist-packages, then reinstall python-bitcoinlib.
brief.standout: Stamping needs no blockchain node or fees: the client sends a digest to free calendar servers, which batch many digests into one Bitcoin transaction, and the proof file carries its own path to the block. The README's Privacy section is unusually candid about metadata leaks, such as timestamps created close together, or several files stamped in one command, which share most of their proof operations.
brief.status: Unknown from the fetched pages. The GitHub page shows no release date, last commit, or version number. The README calls it 'production software that has been in use for many years' and promises the timestamp format will stay verifiable. It lists open issues with no fixes shown, including 'Need unit tests for the client.' The homepage says the default calendars depend on donations.
brief.caveats: Verification needs a local Bitcoin Core node or a calendar's help, and proofs can sit pending for hours. The README says the REST protocol to calendars may change in incompatible ways, so clients must be upgraded. Known issues include: no unit tests; Git re-hashing fails on filenames with invalid Unicode; Git annex works only with the SHA256 and SHA256E backends; Bitcoin RPC errors are not user-friendly; some Python platforms do not check SSL certificates, so calendar connections could be intercepted (though only to produce a proof that fails validation); and ots-git-gpg-wrapper does not check whether the commit timestamp makes sense. Its requirements are Python 3 and Bitcoin Core; the README does not mention Windows. The brew entry had no caveats. The scout notes mention Merkle trees, which the README does not name.
quotes: Command-line tool to create and validate timestamp proofs with the OpenTimestamps protocol, using the Bitcoin blockchain as a timestamp notary.
File contents *are* protected with nonces: a remote calendar learns nothing about the contents of anything you timestamp as it only ever receives an opaque and meaningless digest.
OpenTimestamps is production software that has been in use for many years.
